summary: Reserves an IPv6 unicast address prefix for use in examples in RFCs, books and other documentation. Using it avoids conflicts with real networks, and avoids site-local or link-local addresses, which have special meanings.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 examples need addresses that cannot be confused with real network addresses. This RFC sets aside 2001:DB8::/32 for documentation and says operators should keep it out of routing and packet filters.

questions: what ipv6 address should i use in examples
what ipv6 prefix is reserved for documentation
subtitle: Reserves 2001:DB8::/32 for IPv6 examples in documentation.

tldr.problem: Using real or unallocated IPv6 addresses in examples can conflict with existing or future address assignments when readers copy them into live networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the unicast prefix 2001:DB8::/32 for examples and says it should be treated as non-routable.
tldr.outcome: The prefix is for documentation only, and no end party is to receive an assignment from it. Unit metadata lists RFC 9637 as an update.

today: RFC 3849 is listed as Informational and is updated by RFC 9637, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Documentation Needs Its Own Prefix
sections.content:
Documentation had used IPv6 addresses from blocks already assigned to organizations or from space that might be allocated later. If a reader used such an example in a live network, it could conflict with a real address or route.

Site-local and link-local addresses are unsuitable for many examples, so the RFC reserves a unicast prefix specifically for documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples can cause address conflicts if readers copy real-looking addresses into a network. A reserved prefix gives documentation a distinct set of addresses to use.

sections.title: The Reserved IPv6 Prefix
sections.content:
The prefix reserved for documentation is 2001:DB8::/32. The RFC says it is large enough to let examples match ordinary address-allocation scenarios and can also be used to form documentation multicast addresses using the cited unicast-prefix method.

Representing other kinds of multicast addresses is outside this memo's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Use 2001:DB8::/32 when an IPv6 example needs an address prefix. The RFC also permits using it to form certain multicast examples.

sections.title: Keep the Prefix Out of Routing
sections.content:
IPv6 network operators should add the documentation prefix to their list of non-routable address space. If they use packet filters, they should include the prefix there as well.

The RFC says this is not a local-use prefix and that the filtering advice applies in both local and public contexts. IANA is to record it as documentation-only, with no assignment to an end party.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks should not route this documentation prefix, and packet filters should block it where filters are used. It is reserved for examples rather than assignment to an organization.

references.text: Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Addressing Architecture", RFC 3513, April 2003.
Haberman, B. and D. Thaler, "Unicast-Prefix-based IPv6 Multicast Addresses", RFC 3306, August 2002.
